•
The goal of evaluation is always to rule out a central cause, 
which can have more serious consequences and specific 
management strategies. 
•
Acute vestibular syndrome (AVS) is defined as the sudden onset of 
acute, ‘continuous’ vertigo (lasting longer than 24 hours), 
associated with nausea, vomiting, ataxia, nystagmus, and head 
motion intolerance.  
•
Vestibular neuritis (peripheral cause) and posterior circulation 
stroke (central cause) are the main causes for this syndrome. 
•
If the patient presents with acute vestibular syndrome, APPLY THE 
HINTS bedside examination. 
HINTS EXAM 
HEAD IMPULSE TEST – rapid, passive rotation of 
head while patient fixates on nose of examiner. 
•
Central – no findings (no saccade) 
A normal (negative) exam is worrying 
•
Peripheral – catchup saccade present 
NYSTAGMUS 
•
Central = bilateral, direction changing horizontal 
nystagmus or vertical nystagmus 
•
Peripheral = unilateral, horizontal nystagmus 
TEST OF SKEW = cover/uncover test of each eye 
while patient fixates on nose 
•
Central – refixation present after uncover  
•
Peripheral = no refixation 
CENTRAL CAUSES 
Vertebrobasilar artery insufficiency  
Cerebellar haemorrhage or infarction  
Tumour 
Migrainous vertigo  
Multiple sclerosis  
Post-traumatic injury  
Infection 
Temporal lobe epilepsy  
Subclavian steal syndrome 
 
PERIPHERAL CAUSES 
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) 
Vestibular neuritis  
Labyrinthitis 
Foreign body in ear canal  
Acute otitis media 
Trauma (labyrinth concussion)  
Motion sickness 
Acoustic neuroma  
Meniere’s disease 
 
INVESTIGATIONS 
*HGT 
*ECG 
*Urine ß-HCG 
*Blood gas for electrolytes and Hb 
*Consider LP 
 
CONSIDER CTB 
*Neurological deficit 
*Cerebellar signs 
*Elderly 
*Post trauma
